rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's established practice is to send a messenger before decisively punishing a gravely corrupt nation, so the people have no excuse; Noah warned his people of the imminent punishment and called them to mend their ways.
rows.anchor: it is not punished unless a Messenger is sent by Him to deliver the truth to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's clear warning resembles the naked warner of ancient Arabia who alerted his people to an enemy attack; Noah openly warned them of imminent divine punishment.
rows.anchor: just as a naked warner in ancient Arabia would inform his people of an enemy attack

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā means respecting and observing God's sharīʿah limits throughout life and fearing their breach; those who break them face God's wrath.
rows.anchor: respect and abide by the limits set by the Almighty through His sharī‘ah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obeying Noah means leaving the mischievous leaders for Noah's guidance, since those leaders were taking their followers toward God's punishment.
rows.anchor: people should stop following their mischievous leaders and follow Noah (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's call rests on monotheism, keeping God's sharīʿah, and obeying the prophet; these are the basis of every prophet's call, and a nation strays toward punishment when it abandons them.
rows.anchor: The three basic tenets of Noah’s call are mentioned in this verse: tawḥīd, abiding by the sharī‘ah of God and obedience to the prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the people accept Noah's three tenets, God will forgive the crimes that made them liable to punishment and grant them respite until an appointed time.
rows.anchor: if his people accept these three tenets of Noah’s call the Almighty will forgive their crimes

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some take مِن as redundant; Islahi rejects that analysis because the Qur'an has no superfluous words and Arabic usage gives no supporting example.
rows.anchor: Some people regard the ﻣﻦْ in  to be superfluous ( zā’idah)

rows.speaker: some others
rows.claim: Some others equate مِن with عن; Islahi rejects this view as linguistically unsupported.
rows.anchor: some others regard it to be equivalent in meaning to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects both proposed readings on linguistic grounds: no Qur'anic word is superfluous, and مِن has no attested redundant use in the Qur'an or classical Arabic.
rows.anchor: No word in the Qur’ ān is superfluous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi prefers the ordinary partitive sense of مِن and supplies an understood condition: if the people accept Noah's call, God forgives their earlier sins.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, the verb is in its conventional connotation of tab‘īḍ (partialness).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For sins committed after belief, Islahi invokes 4:17–18: God forgives those who sin while overcome by emotion and quickly repent; he says he explained this principle earlier.
rows.anchor: those who commit a sin while being overwhelmed with emotions and then quickly repent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partitive مِن restricts forgiveness to sins committed in disbelief; embracing faith erases those past sins, not future ones, whereas omitting مِن could wrongly imply forgiveness of both.
rows.anchor: embracing faith after disbelief erases only the pervious sins and not the future ones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to defer punishment means that accepting Noah's three tenets would avert the threatened punishment and give the people a specific period to live.
rows.anchor: the punishment of the Almighty from which Noah (sws) is threatening them with will be deferred by the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An appointed term is finite: even a practicing believer eventually dies, but is spared punitive destruction and allowed to complete the natural lifespan granted to him.
rows.anchor: he is not destroyed by some punishment of the Almighty; he is granted respite to live his full life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A believing nation flourishes while it remains faithful, God-fearing, and obedient to its prophet; deviation brings decline, and moral decadence eventually ends the nation's life.
rows.anchor: its span of life reaches its end, and it is destroyed in its capacity of a nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world itself has a fixed lifespan: the present place of testing will end, and the Hereafter will begin under new laws and regulations.
rows.anchor: a new world – called the Hereafter – with new laws and regulations will come into being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both pious and impious people should remember life's temporary nature: those who use their allotted time with this in mind benefit, while the heedless incur loss through their deeds.
rows.anchor: those who keep this in mind will benefit from the time granted in this life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase wishing that they knew signals that very few understand the secret of success in recognizing life's limited term; Noah expresses this yearning.
rows.anchor: very few people understand this secret. Thus, Noah (sws) has expressed this yearning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects this divine practice to 16:61: if God punished people for their sins, no creature would remain, so He reprieves them to their appointed time, which none can advance or delay.
rows.anchor: If God punished men for their sins, not one creature would be left alive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From v6 begins Noah's second preaching phase and his supplication; as a rasūl, he determines his nation's fate, whose life or death depends on accepting or rejecting him.
rows.anchor: A rasūl decides the fate of his nation in this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's extraordinary preaching duration is supported by 29:14, which says he lived among his people for a thousand years less fifty; the phrase day and night is not exaggeration.
rows.anchor: he dwelt among them for a thousa nd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite his extended efforts, Noah reports that his calls only increased his people's aversion.
rows.anchor: but my calls have only added to their aversion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every messenger calls his people day and night and expends his energy for them, but Noah's unmatched length of effort stands out.
rows.anchor: the lengthy span of time Noah (sws) spent in trying to stir and awaken people from their slumber stands unmatched

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people did not flee because Noah's message lacked reason or because they doubted his honesty; it opposed their desires and their leaders' pride, and their evasions let them avoid changing their lives and face their guilty consciences less.
rows.anchor: The propriety of his message with sense and reason was evident to everyone and everyone also acknowledged the veracity in his heart.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse depicts the people's evasion and arrogance; their repeated flight was an improper scheme for avoiding the truth, but Islahi asks what better strategy truth-fleeing people could adopt.
rows.anchor: This verse portrays the evasion and arrogance of Noah’s people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ellipsis suppresses the phrase about seeking forgiveness; the wording substitutes forgiveness, the result, for seeking it, the action, to expose their wretchedness and refusal even to listen.
rows.anchor: the consequence of an action (forgiveness) was placed in place of the action (seeking forgiveness)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders' drawing their clothes over themselves depicts their haughtiness: they flung shawls over themselves disdainfully and walked away from Noah.
rows.anchor: the arrogance and haughtiness of the leaders of the nation: as soon as they heard Noah’s call

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the coordinated wording, an implied verbal noun after the verb is omitted because a verbal noun appears in the parallel construction.
rows.anchor: a verbal noun is suppressed after the verb
